subject: Variable selection in dynamic occupancy models

messages.author: 99a35bb737ac9f41
messages.subject: Variable selection in dynamic occupancy models
parts:
Hello,

I am sorry, if this question was posted before, but I couldn't seem to find it.

I am relatively new to occupancy modelling and currently trying to fit dynamic occupancy models to camera trap data using unmarked. I have data from 64 camera trap locations that were sampled over 6 years (primary periods) and the presence/absence data was grouped into 16 secondary survey periods (weeks) for at least 6 different species, that I want to model independently from each other, to understand what drove occupancy dynamics.

Now, I am running into some problems trying to fit a model or rather finding the right variables to include in a model. My data includes both Observation Covariates such as climate data and Site Covariates, such as habitat/vegetation data, elevation, distance to urban settlements, etc., that for some sites change between years, therefore I included them as yearlySiteCovs. Before analysis, I checked my variables for multicollinearity and correlation and removed the respective variables from my analysis. I still end up with quite a few potential variables (11 SiteCovs and 4 ObsCovs) for the potential models. 

As I couldn't find a function to do the model selection automatically, I tried to use a backwards elimination approach starting with a global model including all potential variables and removing the most insignificant independent variables, for each detection, occupancy, colonization and extinction, until there is only significant variables left in the model and then fitted a "final" model. Yet, when I analyse the goodness of fit using the mb.gof.test function, it seems that those models are terribly overdispersed, e.g. my Chi² as well as my c-hat values are even Infinite for some species/models. I also tried a more automated modelling approach, where I fit every possible model with every possible combinations of variables and chose the one with the lowest AIC, but the resulting models are even worse. 

There weren't any convergence problems with my models and I only have those major problems for 3 out of 6 species (for the remaining 3 species the backwards elimination approach at least led to models with an okayish GOF, i.e. c-hat < 3). The number of observations for the respective species doesn't seem to be the driving factor here, as those problems occur for species with many observations as well as for species with few observations. 

I am not sure, if my variable selection approach is even the right one or if there is a better way to this, rather than doing a backwards elimination or AIC selection. I would be glad, to receive any suggestions on how I could do this in a way that hopefully helps me find some better models. 

Thank you very much!
Best,
Annika

So I've been reading more about assessing model fit in the respective Chapter of MacKenzie et al. (2017) and I think I have an idea of what causes my problems with calculating Chi² and c-hat. Please, correct me if I got any of this wrong:
As I have 16 secondary survey periods, I have 2^16 (65,635) possible detection histories. Since my number of surveyed units (64) is relatively small compared to the number of possible detection histories, the expected number of cameras with a particular detection history is also extremely small, which results in my huge Chi² values. Additionally, I have a lot of NAs in my dataset due to camera failure/malfunction/theft/etc. Which I guess, increases the number of potential detection histories even more, causing even larger Chi² values and accordingly also huge c-hat values. 

So assuming that this is actually the problem or at least part of the problem, I have two questions:

1. Why do I get much better model fit statistics for some species? The number of survey periods, survey units and missing values is exactly the same for all species, so I don't understand why for some of them the model fit is more or less okay, while for others it is completely terrible. If my theory with the large number of potential detection histories is correct, shouldn't it cause poor model fit for all species? 

2. What can I potentially do to account for this problems? I already grouped the observations into weekly presence/absence data to reduce the number of secondary survey periods. Would it make sense to group it into even larger time intervals (e.g. months) or analyse only a subset of my data, e.g. 6 weeks instead of 16 weeks? 

Thank you very much for your help!
Annika
